bg: corinthians, first epistle to the

Was written from Ephesus (1 Cor. 16:8) about the time of the Passover in the third year of the apostle's sojourn there (Acts 19:10; 20:31), and when he had formed the purpose to visit Macedonia, and then return to Corinth (probably A.D. 57).
Corinth

Some have argued from 2 Cor. 12:14; 13:1, that Paul visited Corinth a third time (i.e., that on some unrecorded occasion he visited the city between what are usually called the first and second visits). But the passages referred to only indicate Paul's intention to visit Corinth (comp. 1 Cor. 16:5, where the Greek present tense denotes an intention), an intention which was in some way frustrated.
Sosthenes

Safe in strength, the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth, who was seized and beaten by the mob in the presence of Gallio, the Roman governor, when he refused to proceed against Paul at the instigation of the Jews (Acts 18:12-17). The motives of this assault against Sosthenes are not recorded, nor is it mentioned whether it was made by Greeks or Romans.
Chloe
Verdure, a female Christian (1 Cor. 1:11), some of whose household had informed Paul of the divided state of the Corinthian church. Nothing is known of her.
ch.s: This chapter covers: A salutation and thanksgiving (vv. 1–9); Exhortation to brotherly love, and reproof for divisions (vv. 10–16); The doctrine of a crucified Saviour, as advancing the glory of God, (vv. 17–25); and humbling the creature before him (vv. 26–31). People named: Paul, Sosthenes, Chloe, Apollos, Cephas, Crispus. Places: Corinth.
ch.mh: All Christians are by baptism dedicated and devoted to Christ, and are under strict obligations to be holy.
q: Read verses 1–9 (A salutation and thanksgiving). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?

Ephesus
The capital of proconsular Asia, which was the western part of Asia Minor. It was colonized principally from Athens.
Adam
Adam and Eve were the progenitors of the whole human race. Evidences of varied kinds are abundant in proving the unity of the human race.
James

The son of Alphaeus, or Cleopas, "the brother" or near kinsman or cousin of our Lord (Gal. 1:18, 19), called James "the Less," or "the Little," probably because he was of low stature. He is mentioned along with the other apostles (Matt. 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:15).

ch.mh: The word resurrection, usually points out our existence beyond the grave.

Macedonia
In New Testament times, was a Roman province lying north of Greece. It was governed by a propraetor with the title of proconsul.
Stephanas

Crown, a member of the church at Corinth, whose family were among those the apostle had baptized (1 Cor. 1:16; 16:15, 17). He has been supposed by some to have been the "jailer of Philippi" (comp. Acts 16:33).
Fortunatus
Fortunate, a disciple of Corinth who visited Paul at Ephesus, and returned with Stephanas and Achaicus, the bearers of the apostle's first letter to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 16:17).

q: Read verses 1–9 (A collection for the poor at Jerusalem). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 10–12 (Timothy and Apollos commended), what do you learn about the church and fellowship?
Verse 13 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Joshua 1:9. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Stephanas’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of love in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of 1 Corinthians?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: By such inquiries, faithfully made, we may judge of the state of our souls.
ch.a: Do one concrete, unannounced act of love for someone in your home or church.
